meta.location: The land of Midian, the land of Ishmael, the land of Nephi
meta.unit: The sons of Mosiah among the Lamanites (Alma 17–26)
principles: A covenant kept at the cost of life

world_behind.title: The war is a civil war
world_behind.text: Verse 1 lists Amalekites, Amulonites, and unconverted Lamanites; verse 2 says they rebelled against their own king. The army coming for the converts is their own nation.

world_behind.title: The old king dies at the hinge
world_behind.text: Verses 3 and 4 have him hand the kingdom to a son named Anti-Nephi-Lehi and die in the same year the war preparations began. The man Aaron taught in Alma 22 never sees the outcome.

world_behind.title: The missionaries call a council on defense
world_behind.text: Verse 5 has Ammon and his brethren gather at Midian and then go to Ishmael to plan with Lamoni and his brother. The chapter's central decision is taken in a war council.

world_behind.title: The refusal precedes the sermon
world_behind.text: Verse 6 states the fact first: not one soul would take up arms, and the king had commanded it. Verses 7 through 16 then give his reasoning to a people who had already decided.

world_behind.title: Their sins were murders
world_behind.text: Verses 9, 10, and 11 name what the correspondence with the Nephites convinced them of. The men putting down weapons are men who had used them on the people they now write letters to.

world_behind.title: The burial is a public assembly
world_behind.text: Verse 17 has all the people gathered, bringing swords and every weapon used for shedding blood, and burying them deep. It is a national act performed at one time.

world_behind.title: The killing has a count
world_behind.text: Verse 22 says a thousand and five were slain, and verse 26 says more than that number joined the same day. Mormon keeps both figures.

words.text: A land where Ammon met his brethren. The name is Moses' place of exile and the nation Gideon fought, and it appears thirty-nine times in the King James Bible. In this record it occurs twice, once inside an Isaiah quotation and once here as a place on the Lamanite map.

A mark left in cloth that will not wash out. Three of the record's four uses are in this king's speech, where sin stains and God takes the stain away. The fourth is Alma 5, where no one is saved whose garments are not washed white. The image runs from the cloth to the sword and back.

Giving one's word as surety. It appears once in scripture. Mormon pairs it with covenanting to describe what the people did as they buried the weapons, which makes the burial a legal act witnessed by the whole nation.

A bodily posture held on purpose. The record uses it five times and the King James Bible never. Lehi and Alma both see angels in the attitude of singing; here a nation is in the attitude of prostration and prayer while swords come down on them.

Pierced, wounded to the quick. The word occurs once in this record. Alma 22 had Aaron telling a king that the sting of death is swallowed up; here the attackers are stung for their own murders and throw down their weapons.

Given light, brought to understand. The record uses it three times and the King James Bible six, and Hebrews 6 builds the same warning out of it: those once enlightened who fall away are in the worse case. Mormon closes the chapter with that doctrine and the Amalekites as the example.

phrases.term: There was not one soul... that would take up arms against their brethren
phrases.text: Mormon reports unanimity before he reports the reasoning. Every convert refused, and their king backed the refusal with a command. The decision was already whole when the speech began.

phrases.term: We have opened a correspondence with these brethren, the Nephites
phrases.text: The king thanks God for letters. Alma 23 ended with the correspondence; here he treats it as the instrument that convinced them of their sins. Contact did the work that centuries of war had not.

phrases.term: As we were the most lost of all mankind
phrases.text: A king says it of his own nation, in public, as the premise of an argument. The self-assessment is the reason he gives for taking no chances with a relapse.

He moves the image from the heart to the blade. God took away the stains; the swords are clean; therefore they stay clean. The whole case for burying the weapons runs on one metaphor held consistently.

phrases.term: Perhaps, if we should stain our swords again they can no more be washed bright
phrases.text: The reasoning is cautious and the king marks it as uncertain. He says perhaps. The covenant is built on a fear he cannot verify, and the record keeps the hedge in his mouth.

phrases.term: Let us hide them away that they may be kept bright, as a testimony to our God at the last day
phrases.text: The buried swords are evidence for a future hearing. They are put out of reach so that they can be produced later, unused, as proof of what the people did with the years they had.

phrases.term: Rather than spend their days in idleness they would labor abundantly with their hands
phrases.text: The covenant has three clauses and only the first is about killing. They also bind themselves to give instead of taking and to work instead of resting. Alma 23 had already called them industrious.

phrases.term: They buried their weapons of peace, or they buried the weapons of war, for peace
phrases.text: Mormon writes the sentence twice because he is correcting himself mid-line. The slip is preserved on the plates, and it says what he means better than the fix does.

phrases.term: Praised God even in the very act of perishing under the sword
phrases.text: This is what the attackers saw. A people going down under the sword and singing on the way. Verse 24 says the sight is what stopped the killing.

phrases.term: Relying upon the mercies of those whose arms were lifted to slay them
phrases.text: The men who threw down their weapons put themselves in the position of the people they had been killing. Mormon describes the surrender in the exact terms of the thing that converted them.

phrases.term: Their state becomes worse than though they had never known these things
phrases.text: Mormon's own conclusion, drawn from the Amalekites and Amulonites. He attaches it to the hard fact of verse 29: every convert that day descended from Laman and Lemuel, and none from the dissenters.

verses.label: v. 1–4
verses.title: The rebellion
verses.text: The unconverted, stirred by Amalekites and Amulonites, turn on their own king and take up arms against the converts. The king gives the kingdom to his son, names him Anti-Nephi-Lehi, and dies the same year the war preparations begin.

verses.label: v. 5–6
verses.title: The council, and the refusal
verses.text: Ammon gathers his brethren at Midian and comes to Ishmael to plan a defense with Lamoni and the new king. Mormon states the outcome first: no convert would take up arms, and the king had forbidden it.

verses.label: v. 7–11
verses.title: The thanksgiving
verses.text: Four times the king thanks God: for the Nephite missionaries, for a softened heart and an open correspondence, for conviction of their murders, and for forgiveness through the merits of the Son. Then he calls his people the most lost of all mankind.

verses.label: v. 12–16
verses.title: The case for burying them
verses.text: God took away the stains and the swords are bright. Staining them again might put washing out of reach. So hide them, keep them bright as a testimony at the judgment, and if the brethren destroy us we go to God saved.

verses.label: v. 17–19
verses.title: The burial and the covenant
verses.text: The whole people assemble, bring every weapon used for shedding blood, and bury them deep. They vouch and covenant to give up their lives before shedding blood, to give instead of taking, and to work instead of idling.

verses.label: v. 20–25
verses.title: The slaughter, and the turning
verses.text: The army comes to kill the king and destroy the people. The converts go out to meet them, prostrate themselves, and pray. A thousand and five are killed without resistance. The attackers see them praising God as they die, stop, and throw down their own weapons.

verses.label: v. 26–30
verses.title: The count and the lesson
verses.text: More joined that day than were killed. Not one wicked man died. The killers were mostly Amalekites and Amulonites of the order of Nehor, and not one of the new converts came from those groups. Mormon draws his conclusion about falling away.

chapter.title: The decision is made in a war council
chapter.text: Ammon and the kings meet to discuss defense, and the answer that comes out is a burial. The record frames the refusal as a strategic conclusion reached by people with the option of fighting.

chapter.title: The argument turns on relapse
chapter.text: The king's case is that they might not survive a second repentance. He wants the means of the old sin put permanently out of reach, and the weapons are buried for that reason.

chapter.title: Uncertainty is left in the reasoning
chapter.text: Verse 13 says perhaps. The king does not claim to know whether a second forgiveness would come. He acts on the risk, and the record does not upgrade his caution into knowledge.

chapter.title: The covenant covers three habits
chapter.text: Blood, property, and work. The famous clause is the first, and the people bound themselves to generosity and labor in the same breath.

chapter.title: Mormon's correction stays in the text
chapter.text: Weapons of peace, then weapons of war for peace. He caught the phrase going wrong and fixed it on the plate without erasing the first version.

chapter.title: What stopped the killing was worship
chapter.text: Verse 23 names the thing the attackers could not get past: people praising God while dying under the sword. The chapter locates the persuasion in the singing.

chapter.title: The arithmetic is kept
chapter.text: A thousand and five dead, more than that converted the same day, no wicked man among the slain. Mormon gives the numbers and lets the reader do the sum.

chapter.title: The dissenters supply the closing doctrine
chapter.text: No Amalekite or Amulonite joined, and every convert descended from Laman and Lemuel. Mormon turns the demographic fact into the warning about knowing and then falling away.

applications.title: Put the means out of reach
applications.text: They buried the swords deep instead of storing them somewhere safe. Where you have repented of something, ask what would have to be physically gone for a relapse to be difficult, and go make it gone.

applications.title: Say what you are grateful for before you say what you have decided
applications.text: The king listed four mercies before he asked anything of his people. When you have a hard call to explain, start with what has already been given.

applications.title: Bind yourself to the positive clause too
applications.text: The covenant included giving and working alongside the refusal. When you commit to stopping something, name the thing you will do with the time and the means it frees.

applications.title: Let people see what you do under pressure
applications.text: The attackers were changed by what they saw, and nobody preached at them. Where you are being treated badly, the observable part of your response is doing more work than any explanation you could offer.

questions.text: What relationship has changed because someone finally opened a channel?
What would I say if I had to name the worst of what I have been?
What am I unwilling to risk because I am not sure I would recover from it?
If something of mine had to be produced at the judgment as evidence, what would I want it to be?
What have I stopped doing without ever deciding what to do instead?
Whose mercy have I had to rely on after being in the wrong?
What do I know that I am currently living beneath?
